title: Which statements describe this mechanism? Circle all that apply
asks: Statements about rate law, stereochemistry and solvent are listed. Circle every one that is (or is not) true of the mechanism.

know.h: The number in the name is the molecularity: how many species take part in the rate-determining step. {{SN2}} and {{E2}} are bimolecular, {{SN1}} and {{E1}} are unimolecular.
know.from: Lecture 11/03, p. 3; Lecture 11/10, p. 1 and 4; Lecture 11/12, p. 1

know.h: Rate laws. {{SN2}}: rate = k[nucleophile][substrate]. {{E2}}: rate = k[substrate][base]. {{SN1}} and {{E1}}: rate = k[substrate] only. Doubling the nucleophile or base doubles the rate of {{SN2}} and {{E2}} and does nothing to {{SN1}} and {{E1}}.
know.from: Rate tables: Lecture 11/03, p. 3; 11/10, p. 1; 11/12, p. 1

know.h: Steps and intermediates. {{SN2}} and {{E2}} are concerted: one step, one transition state, no intermediate, one hump on the energy diagram. {{SN1}} and {{E1}} go through a carbocation intermediate: at least two humps with a valley between, and the first hump (ionization) is the highest.
{{SN1}} and {{E1}} share the same carbocation. They compete: {{SN1}} is favored at lower temperature, {{E1}} at high temperature.

Stereochemistry of substitution. {{SN2}} gives inversion at the electrophilic carbon: one enantiomer gives one enantiomer. {{SN1}} gives racemization, because the planar carbocation is attacked from either face.
Stereochemistry of {{E2}}. The hydrogen removed and the leaving group must be anti-periplanar. The lecture calls this the most important factor for {{E2}}.

Substrate order. {{SN2}}: methyl > primary > secondary, and tertiary does not react (steric hindrance). {{SN1}} and {{E1}}: tertiary > secondary, and primary and methyl do not react (carbocation stability). {{E2}} works with tertiary, secondary and primary substrates, but not methyl, which has no neighbouring hydrogen.
Allyl and vinyl. An allyl substrate does {{SN2}} (relative rate 1.3) and {{SN1}}. A vinyl substrate does neither.

Nucleophile and base strength. {{SN2}} needs a good nucleophile. {{E2}} needs a strong base. {{SN1}} and {{E1}} work with a poor nucleophile or weak base such as water, because that species arrives after the slow step.
Solvent. {{SN1}} and {{E1}} are favored by polar protic solvents (water, alcohols), and a more polar solvent makes {{SN1}} faster. {{SN2}} is favored by polar aprotic solvents (DMSO, DMF, acetone).
Leaving group. Every one of the four mechanisms needs a good leaving group (iodide, bromide, chloride, tosylate). Hydroxide and fluoride are poor leaving groups.
Rearrangement can happen only when there is a carbocation: in {{SN1}} and {{E1}}, never in {{SN2}} or {{E2}}.

Which alkene. {{E2}} usually gives mainly the more substituted (Saytzeff) alkene: 81% with iodide, 72% with bromide, 67% with chloride for 2-hexyl. With fluoride the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene is the major one, 70%.

Skill: read the question's direction. The exam asks either which statements are characteristics or which are NOT. Decide true or false for every statement first, then circle the set the question asks for.

method: Underline the mechanism named and the word IS or NOT in the question.
Write the mechanism's short list in the margin: rate law, one step or carbocation, stereochemistry, best substrate, nucleophile or base needed, best solvent.
Mark each statement true or false for that mechanism, one at a time, without thinking yet about what to circle.
For a false statement, name the mechanism it does belong to. This catches statements that are true of {{SN2}} but offered for {{SN1}}.
Circle the true ones if the question asks what the mechanism is, the false ones if it asks what it is NOT. Several answers, or only one, may be right.

pitfalls.h: Circling the true statements when the question asks for the ones that are NOT characteristics.
Giving {{SN1}} the properties of {{SN2}}: inversion, or a rate that depends on the nucleophile.
Thinking the solvent does not matter for {{SN1}}. A more polar, protic solvent speeds up the ionization.
Mixing up {{E1}} and {{E2}}: {{E2}} needs a strong base and has the base in its rate law, {{E1}} does neither.
Saying that tertiary substrates are unreactive in every bimolecular reaction. They cannot do {{SN2}}, but they do {{E2}} readily.
Stopping after the first correct statement. Circle all that apply.
